publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the human cell types themselves - a reference atlas defining them by molecular profile and connecting that to classical description
span.quote: The Human Cell Atlas Project is an international collaborative effort that aims to define all human cell types in terms of distinctive molecular profiles (such as gene expression profiles) and to connect this information with classical cellular descriptions (such as location and morphology).

span.label: whether all human cell types can be identified and defined by molecular profile, 150 years after the effort began
span.quote: The recent advent of methods for high-throughput single-cell molecular profiling has catalyzed a growing sense in the scientific community that the time is ripe to complete the 150-year-old effort to identify all cell types in the human body.

span.label: a design for a comprehensive cell atlas WHICH DECLINES TO DEFINE ITS OWN CENTRAL TERM: the definition of `cell type` is deferred to empirical observation on purpose, and the reasons are stated
span.quote: For all the reasons above, we have not attempted to propose a precise definition of 'cell type'. Rather, the definition should evolve based on empirical observation.

span.label: method
span.quote: An open comprehensive reference map of the molecular state of cells in healthy human tissues would propel the systematic study of physiological states, developmental trajectories, regulatory circuitry and interactions of cells, and also provide a framework for understanding cellular dysregulation in human disease.

span.label: cells as points in a high-dimensional molecular space, where similar cells are close but never identical
span.quote: Thus, a cell 'type' might be defined as a region or a probability distribution ( Kim and Eberwine, 2010; Sul et al., 2012) either in the full-dimensional space or in a projection onto a lower-dimensional space that reflects salient features. While this notion is intuitively compelling, it is challenging to give a precise definition of a 'cell type'.

span.label: single-cell genomic profiling at scale, with unsupervised clustering as an initial framework for discovering types
span.term: single-cell genomic profiling at scale, with unsupervised clustering as an initial framework for discovering types
span.quote: However, only in the past few years has it begun to seem feasible to undertake the kind of systematic, high-resolution characterization of human cells necessary to create a systematic cell atlas. The key has been the recent ability to apply genomic profiling approaches to single cells.

span.label: a cell TYPE is proposed as a REGION or a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION in the full-dimensional molecular space or a projection of it - the category becomes a geometry rather than a list of properties
span.quote: Thus, a cell 'type' might be defined as a region or a probability distribution ( Kim and Eberwine, 2010; Sul et al., 2012) either in the full-dimensional space or in a projection onto a lower-dimensional space that reflects salient features. While this notion is intuitively compelling, it is challenging to give a precise definition of a 'cell type'.

span.label: types discovered as regions in feature space are then to be DISTILLED into simple molecular and morphological signatures, so that independent laboratories can index and compare cells at all
span.quote: Whereas cell types are initially defined based on regions in feature space, it will be important eventually to distill them into simpler molecular and morphological signatures that can be used to index cells in the atlas, aggregate and compare results from independent labs and different individuals, and create tools and reagents for validation and follow up studies.

span.label: THE PROJECT DECLINES TO DEFINE ITS CENTRAL TERM AND SAYS SO: `we have not attempted to propose a precise definition of cell type. Rather, the definition should evolve based on empirical observation` - in a paper whose stated aim is to define all human cell types
span.quote: For all the reasons above, we have not attempted to propose a precise definition of 'cell type'. Rather, the definition should evolve based on empirical observation.

span.label: the field lacks a rigorous definition of BOTH `cell type` and `cell state`, and the boundary between them is blurred because cells change over time in ways not fully understood
span.quote: At a conceptual level, one challenge is that we lack a rigorous definition of what we mean by the intuitive terms 'cell type' and 'cell state'. Cell type often implies a notion of persistence ( _e.g._, being a hepatic stellate cell or a cerebellar Purkinje cell), while cell state often refers to more transient properties ( _e.g._, being in the G1 phase of the cell cycle or experiencing nutrient deprivation). But, the boundaries between these concepts can be blurred, because cells change over time in ways that are far from fully understood.

span.label: THE TAXONOMY MAY NOT BE A TAXONOMY: finer distinctions may not obey a strict hierarchy, some distinctions are graded rather than discrete, and IT REMAINS UNCLEAR WHETHER THE MORPHOLOGICAL, MOLECULAR AND PHYSIOLOGICAL AXES AGREE WITH EACH OTHER
span.quote: Cell-type taxonomies are often represented as hierarchies based on morphological, physiological, and molecular differences ( Sanes and Masland, 2015). Whereas higher distinctions are easily agreed upon, finer ones may be less obvious and may not obey a strict hierarchy, either because distinct types share features, or because some distinctions are graded and not discrete. Critically, it remains unclear whether distinctions based on morphological, molecular and physiological properties agree with each other.

span.label: the existing molecular classification is AD HOC - built on markers discovered by accident or chosen for convenience rather than systematically
span.quote: In addition, molecular classification of cells has largely been ad hoc – based on markers discovered by accident or chosen for convenience – rather than systematic and comprehensive.

span.label: clustering supplies only a starting framework: the `right` features, the `right` similarity metric and the `right` level of granularity are all open, and the paper puts each of the three in scare quotes
span.quote: Unsupervised clustering algorithms for high-dimensional data provide an initial framework ( Grün et al., 2015; Grün et al., 2016; Jaitin et al., 2014; Levine et al., 2015; Macosko et al., 2015; Shekhar et al., 2016; Vallejos et al., 2015), but substantial advances will be needed in order to select the 'right' features, the 'right' similarity metric, and the 'right' level of granularity for the question at hand, control for distinct biological processes, handle technical noise, and connect novel clusters with legacy knowledge.

span.label: the full lineage tree from zygote to adult is known for exactly one organism - C. elegans, transparent, with about 1,000 cells
span.quote: Even less is known about cell states and their relationships during development: the full lineage tree of cells from the single-cell zygote to the adult is only known for the nematode _C. elegans_, which is transparent and has just ~1000 cells.

span.label: the definition of `cell type` is deferred to empirical observation rather than fixed in advance, and the deferral is stated as a decision with its reasons
span.note: eliminates: a catalogue whose categories were settled before the data that was supposed to produce them - and the paper's own reasons are that the hierarchy may not hold, the distinctions may be graded, and the axes may not agree · outcome: held
